transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, my mom... she's the one who set this up, because she keeps coming into my room and asking what's wrong, just standing in the doorway asking me over and over, and I... I barely even have the energy to answer her anymore. It's like my voice is just gone, or it's too heavy to push out of my throat. Mostly I just can't make myself do anything at all anymore. I just sit in my room. For hours, really, just sitting there on the edge of the bed or staring at the wall, wearing the exact same clothes I had on yesterday, and the day before that. It's just... taking them off and putting new ones on is like climbing a mountain, so I just stay in the same sweatpants and the same shirt. 

I used to do things, you know? I used to knit, I had this whole basket of different colored yarns and I'd make these really complicated patterns, and I used to journal every single day, filling up notebooks with my handwriting, and I'd go walking down the street every afternoon just to get out of the house and feel the air. But now the yarn just sits there getting dusty, and the journals are closed, and I don't go outside. I just sit. And when my mom asks why I'm not doing my knitting or why I'm in the same clothes again, I just... I can't even explain it to her, I just don't have the energy to form the words to tell her that I just can't make myself move or care.
Do you still enjoy the things you used to, like knitting or going for walks?

No, I don't. I really don't. It's like... it's like the part of my brain that used to feel good about things just turned off, or dried up, or something. I look at my knitting basket—it's right there in the corner of my room, full of all this beautiful, soft yarn, the merino wool I used to save up my allowance to buy, all these bright blues and deep greens—and I just feel absolutely nothing. Not a spark, not a tiny little urge to pick up the needles. It's just stuff taking up space now. 

And the walks... I used to love the way the air felt, especially when it was getting close to evening and the streetlights would just start flickering on, turning that weird orangey-pink color. I'd walk all the way down to the end of our subdivision and back, just listening to my shoes on the pavement. But now? The thought of even standing up, of finding my shoes, of tying the laces, of opening the front door... it's just so exhausting. I can't make myself do it. I can't make myself do anything. 

That's why I'm in these same clothes, these gray sweatpants with the little hole near the knee and this faded blue t-shirt. My mom came in again this morning, standing right there in the doorway, holding a stack of clean laundry, and she looked at me and said, "Honey, are you ever going to change? Are you ever going to pick up your knitting again?" And I just sat there on the edge of the mattress. I tried to think of an answer, I really did, I tried to pull the words up from my chest, but I just... I barely have the energy to even open my mouth anymore. I just stared at her until she sighed and put the laundry on my dresser and walked out. I just don't care about the yarn, or the walks, or the journals, or the clean clothes. I just don't have it in me.
How long have you been feeling this way?

It's... well, it's been a really long time. A really, really long time. I remember exactly when it started, actually, because it was right when I was supposed to be starting this whole new chapter of my life. It was about two years and two months ago. I had just enrolled in this community college program, you know? I was supposed to be taking these general ed classes, English and History and this introductory psychology course that I thought I was going to be so interested in. I had all my notebooks bought—the nice ones, the spiral-bound ones with the thick paper, color-coded for each subject—and I had my pens all lined up in my pencil case. 

But then... it just started slipping. Right from the beginning of that semester, two years and two months ago. At first, I thought I was just tired from the transition, you know, going from high school to college, even if it was just the community college down the road. I told myself, "Oh, you're just adjusting, everyone gets tired." But then it wasn't just being tired. It was this... this heavy feeling, like my bones were turning into lead. I'd sit in the lecture hall for that History class—it was on Tuesdays and Thursdays at 10 AM, in this room that always smelled faintly of floor wax and old coffee—and I'd just stare at the professor's mouth moving, and I couldn't make myself care about what he was saying. I couldn't make myself take notes. The blue notebook just sat there on the desk, closed. 

And then it just kept getting worse from there. That whole decline, it just kept going down and down. I stopped going to the classes. I couldn't get out of bed to make it to the 10 AM one, and then I couldn't even make it to the afternoon ones. And it's just been like that ever since. For over two years now, just this slow, endless slide into... into nothing. Two years and two months of just sitting here, watching the yarn get dusty and wearing the same sweatpants, while everyone else from my high school is out there doing things, and I'm just... stuck. I've been stuck since that very first week of classes.
Do you ever experience any pleasure or enjoyment in your daily life?

No, I don't. I really don't think I do. It's like I was saying before, about the knitting and the walks... it's all just gone. The pleasure is just gone. I wake up in the morning, and the light comes through the blinds—those cheap plastic blinds in my room that always get tangled if you try to pull them up, so I just leave them down—and I look at the dust motes floating in the little slivers of sunlight, and I just feel... flat. Completely flat. 

I don't look forward to breakfast, I don't care what my mom makes. She could make my favorite, those blueberry pancakes she used to do on Sundays with the real maple syrup, and it would just taste like cardboard to me now. I just don't get any joy out of it. Mostly I just can't make myself do anything anymore. I just sit there in my room, on the edge of the bed, wearing the exact same clothes I had on yesterday, those gray sweatpants and the faded blue t-shirt. I don't knit, even though the basket is right there. I don't open my journals. I don't go walking down the street to see the streetlights come on. 

And my mom... she comes in, and she stands there, and she looks at me with this worried expression, her eyebrows all pinched together, and she asks me what's wrong, why I'm just sitting there, why I'm not doing anything fun. And I just... I barely have the energy to answer her. I can't even explain that there is no fun anymore. There's no enjoyment. There's just me, sitting in the room, existing, while the yarn gets dusty and the days just kind of blur together into one long, gray stretch of nothing. I don't feel happy, I don't feel excited, I don't feel... anything good. It's just empty.
Have you ever thought about hurting yourself or ending your life?

No, no... I don't think about that. I mean, I know people get sad and they think about those things, but for me, it's not like a sharp sadness that makes you want to do something drastic. It's just... it's just that heavy, flat feeling I was telling you about. 

I just sit there on the edge of the mattress, looking at the little hole in the knee of my sweatpants—it's on the left knee, just a tiny tear where the fabric got thin, but I pick at the threads sometimes when I'm just staring into space—and I don't think about hurting myself. I don't think about ending it all, because even thinking about something like that, making a plan, figuring out how to do it... that takes energy. That takes some kind of drive or motivation, and I just don't have any of that left. My bones are lead, remember? 

I just want to sit there. I don't want to die, but I don't really feel like I'm living either, you know? I'm just sort of suspended in this gray area. My mom will come in, and she'll look at me, and I know she's probably terrified that I'm going to do something to myself, because she reads all those articles online about depression and things like that, but I'm not going to. I just don't have it in me to do anything at all, let alone something that big. I just watch the dust motes in the sunlight and wait for the day to be over so I can go back to sleep, even though I'm not really tired in the normal way, just... exhausted by existing. So, no, I don't think about hurting myself. I just don't think about much of anything anymore.
Do you find that your movements or reactions have slowed down?

I... I don't know. I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, I'm not moving around much anyway, like I said. I'm just sitting on the bed. So how would I even know if I'm moving slower? When I do get up to go to the bathroom—it's just down the hall, past the linen closet with the squeaky hinge that my dad was supposed to fix before he left—I don't feel like I'm walking in slow motion or anything. It's just... I'm just walking. 

I guess maybe it takes me a long time to decide to get up, but once I'm actually moving, it's just normal walking. It's not like I'm dragging my feet on purpose, even though they feel heavy. And my reactions... I don't know what you mean by that, really. Like if someone threw a ball at me? Nobody is throwing balls at me. I'm just in my room. My mom talks to me, and I answer her eventually, but it's not because I can't physically speak faster. It's just because I don't have anything to say, and it takes so much effort to pull the words together and push them out of my mouth. 

So, no, I don't think my actual movements are slow. It's just the deciding to move that's hard. Like yesterday, I needed a glass of water, and I looked at the empty cup on my nightstand—it's this blue plastic cup we got from a pizza place years ago—and I knew I needed to take it to the kitchen to fill it up, but I just stared at it for maybe an hour before I actually reached out my hand. But when I finally reached out, my hand moved at a normal speed, I think. I just... I haven't noticed anything being actually slow, just... stuck. Everything is just stuck.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past two years?

I don't... I don't really think so. I haven't stepped on a scale in a long time. We have one in the bathroom, it's one of those older mechanical ones with the dial that spins around, you know? It's white, but the little black rubber mat on top is peeling up at the corners because the steam from the shower ruined the glue years ago. I just look at it on the floor next to the sink when I go in there, but I never actually stand on it. There's just no reason to. 

But I know I haven't lost a bunch of weight because my clothes all fit exactly the same way they always have. Those gray sweatpants I was telling you about, the ones with the little hole in the left knee? The elastic in the waistband still feels exactly the same against my stomach as it did when my mom bought them. She got them at Target on clearance, actually, a couple of years ago, and she was so happy about saving money. 

And even though I told you the food doesn't taste like anything anymore, even though her cooking just feels like chewing on wet cardboard now, I still eat whatever she brings me. She'll bring a plate into my room and set it on the nightstand right next to that blue plastic cup, and I'll eventually eat it just because it's sitting there and it's easier to just chew and swallow than to have her come back in and ask me why I'm not eating. She gets so worried, her voice gets all high-pitched and shaky, and I just don't have the energy to deal with that, to try and explain that I'm not hungry but I'm not starving myself either. So I eat the cardboard food, and I sit on the mattress, and I don't lose weight. I'm just exactly the same size, taking up the exact same amount of space in the room as I did two years ago. Nothing changes. So, no, I haven't lost weight. I'm just the same.
Do you feel like you're a burden to your family or the people around you?

I don't... I don't really know if I feel like a burden. I mean, what does that even mean, really? Like a heavy sack of rocks someone has to carry around? I guess I am heavy, like I said, my bones feel like lead, but it's not like my mom is physically carrying me. 

She just brings me the plates of food, and she washes those gray sweatpants when I finally take them off, and she stands in the doorway looking at me with that worried expression. Her eyebrows always scrunch together right in the middle, making this little crease above her nose, and she sighs a lot. She sighs when she picks up the empty blue plastic cup, and she sighs when she opens my curtains to let the sunlight in, even though I just close them again as soon as she leaves because the light is too bright and it makes my eyes hurt. 

I guess maybe she feels like I'm a burden, because she has to do those things for me, but I never asked her to. I never said, "Mom, please bring me food that tastes like cardboard and wash my clothes." She just does it because she's my mom, and I think that's what moms do, right? They take care of you, even when you're nineteen and you should be out getting a job or going to college or doing whatever normal people do instead of just sitting on a mattress picking at a hole in your sweatpants. 

But I don't actively think to myself, "I am a burden." I just think about how tired I am. I think about how much energy it takes just to exist in this room, breathing the air and watching the dust motes. If I'm a burden, it's just a passive thing, like a piece of furniture that's in the way but nobody has the energy to move it out to the garage. I'm just here, taking up space, and she's just dealing with it. So, I don't know if I feel like a burden. I just feel... here. Just stuck here.
Do you wish you could be around other people or engage in social activities?

I don't... I don't really wish for that. I mean, to wish for something, you have to actually want to do it, and I just... mostly I just can't make myself do anything anymore. It's not even about other people, really. It's just about doing anything at all. I just sit in my room, usually right here on the edge of the mattress, with the exact same clothes on. Those same gray sweatpants with the hole in the knee that I told you about. I don't even change my shirt. It's just this oversized blue t-shirt with a faded logo from a summer camp I went to in middle school, and I just wear it day after day because taking it off and pulling a new one over my head requires a kind of energy that I just don't possess right now. 

I don't even do the things I used to like doing by myself, so the idea of a social activity is just... it's impossible to even picture. I used to knit, you know? I have this big woven basket of yarn sitting right next to my bed. I was working on this thick, cable-knit scarf with this mustard-yellow yarn because I thought it would look nice in the fall, but the basket is just sitting there gathering dust. The wooden needles are still stuck right in the middle of a row. I haven't touched it in months. And I don't journal anymore, either. I have a stack of notebooks on my desk, those spiral ones with the college-ruled paper, and I used to write down everything, every little thought or thing that happened, but now the pens just sit in the mug on my desk and I don't even look at them. I don't go walking like I used to, either. I used to walk down to the park at the end of our subdivision, just to look at the oak trees and get out of the house, but now just the thought of finding my sneakers and tying the laces feels like trying to climb a mountain. 

So, being around people... I don't know how I would even do that. When my mom comes into my room and she asks what's wrong—she stands there in the doorway with that crease between her eyebrows that I mentioned, and she asks me, "Honey, what's wrong? Why won't you do anything?"—I barely even have the energy to answer her. I just look at her, and my mouth feels like it's glued shut. It takes everything I have inside me just to push out the words "I don't know" or "I'm fine." So if I can't even muster the energy to form a complete sentence for my own mother who is standing right in front of me, how could I possibly go to a social activity? I wouldn't be able to talk to anyone. I wouldn't be able to participate. I would just be sitting there, completely stuck, just like I'm stuck here in this room. So no, I don't wish to be around people. I don't really wish for anything at all.
Do you often feel guilty about your current situation or the fact that you're not doing the things you used to?

I don't... I don't think I feel guilty. Guilt is a really sharp feeling, isn't it? Like a twisting in your stomach or a tightness in your throat. I remember what it used to feel like. When I was a sophomore in high school, I accidentally knocked my mom's favorite coffee mug off the kitchen counter. It was this heavy ceramic one with a hand-painted sunflower on it that she bought at a craft fair years ago, and it shattered into a million pieces all over the linoleum. I felt so incredibly guilty then. My chest got all tight and hot, and I cried the whole time I was sweeping up the little yellow and brown pieces. 

But now... I don't feel anything like that. When I look over at that big woven basket with the mustard-yellow yarn and the wooden needles just sticking out of it, I don't feel bad that I stopped. I just look at it and register that it's there. It's just an object gathering dust, just like the notebooks on my desk. My mom will come in with that forced, overly cheerful voice—the one she uses when she's trying really hard not to sound worried—and she'll say things like, "Why don't you try doing just one row of your scarf today, honey?" And I know, logically, that a normal person would feel guilty for disappointing her, for just sitting here in this same blue camp t-shirt staring at the wall instead of being the daughter she wants. 

But the guilt just isn't there. It's like that part of my brain just dried up. There's just a big, blank emptiness where feelings like guilt are supposed to live. I think it takes too much energy to feel guilty, honestly. You have to actually care about how things are supposed to be in order to feel bad that they aren't that way, and I just... I don't care. I don't care about the scarf, or the park down the street, or the fact that I'm nineteen and doing absolutely nothing with my life. It's just the way it is now. So, no, I don't feel guilty. I don't really feel much of anything.
Do you ever find any activities or things that used to bring you pleasure are now not enjoyable at all?

I mean... I guess that goes back to what I was just saying. It's exactly like I was telling you before, mostly I just can't make myself do anything anymore. Pleasure isn't even a concept that makes sense to me right now. I sit in my room with the exact same clothes on—this same blue camp shirt and those gray sweatpants, day in and day out—and the thought of doing something for "fun" is just... it's completely alien to me. 

I don't knit, I don't journal, I don't go walking like I used to. And I used to really love those things, I really did. I used to love the way the pen scratched on the college-ruled paper when I was writing down my thoughts, or the way the air smelled down at the park under those big oak trees, especially after it rained. It used to make me feel something. A lightness, maybe. But now? If I were to pick up that mustard-yellow yarn from the basket, it wouldn't feel nice or cozy. It wouldn't feel like anything. It would just feel like holding two heavy, pointless wooden sticks. There's no joy in it. There's no joy in anything at all. It's all just completely flat. 

And when my mom comes in and asks what's wrong, when she stands in the doorway trying to figure out why I dropped all these hobbies I used to spend hours on... I barely have the energy to answer her. I just look at her, and my head feels like it's packed full of wet sand. It takes so much physical effort just to breathe and exist on that mattress, let alone try to explain to her that the things that used to make me happy just... don't register for me anymore. So, yeah, I don't find them enjoyable. I don't find anything enjoyable. I just sit there.
Do you feel like your thoughts are moving slowly?

I don't... I don't think they're moving slowly. I mean, to have slow thoughts, you'd have to actually be having thoughts to begin with, right? And I just... I don't really have much going on up there to measure the speed of. 

When I'm sitting there on the edge of my mattress in these same gray sweatpants, just staring at the wall or looking over at that basket of mustard-yellow yarn, it's not like my brain is trying to process things and just taking a really long time to do it. It's not like when I was in high school and I'd be sitting in Mr. Harrison's algebra class, staring at a complicated equation on the whiteboard, and feeling like my brain was trudging through thick mud trying to figure out the answer. It's not like that at all. It's just... it's more like a blankness. 

Like I said before about my head feeling like it's full of wet sand, it's heavy, but it's not... it's not slow. I hear things right away. When my mom stands in the doorway with that crease between her eyebrows and says, "Honey, what's wrong?" I understand her immediately. The words don't take a long time to reach me. I process exactly what she's asking the second she says it. It's just that once the words land, there's no answering thought that comes after. There's just nothing. 

So I wouldn't say my thoughts are slow. I don't really notice them being slow at all. It's just that there aren't many of them anymore. I just sit there and look at the dust gathering on my desk, or the pens sitting in that mug, and my mind is just kind of... quiet. Not moving slowly, just... not really moving much at all, because there's nothing there to move.
Do you feel like it takes you a long time to react to things that are happening around you?

I don't... I don't really think so. I mean, it's not like my reflexes are broken or I'm moving in slow motion or anything like that. I haven't noticed any kind of delay. 

Like, just yesterday afternoon, I was sitting on my mattress—right in the exact same spot I always sit, kind of near the window where the blinds are pulled shut because the glare from the street is always too bright—and my cell phone started ringing. It was sitting on the wooden nightstand right next to me, right beside this old digital alarm clock I've had since middle school, the one with the red numbers that are honestly way too bright at night. Anyway, the ringtone went off. It was just that loud, default chime, and I reacted right away. I turned my head the very second it started. I didn't sit there for a minute trying to figure out what the sound was. I looked at the screen immediately, saw it lighting up, and saw it was my Aunt Linda calling. She always calls on Tuesdays around three because she gets off work early from the dental clinic. 

I knew it was her, and I saw it instantly. I didn't answer it, obviously. I just watched the screen light up and vibrate against the wood until it finally went to voicemail. But the actual reaction? Noticing that it was happening? That was instant. If a car honks out on the street, I flinch just as fast as anyone else. If my mom drops a spoon on the linoleum in the kitchen downstairs, I hear the clatter right away and I know exactly what the sound is. There's no lag, you know? Like a computer freezing up or something. It's nothing like that. I see and hear everything in real-time, exactly when it happens. I just... I just don't have any desire to do anything about the things happening around me. But the reacting part itself doesn't take a long time at all.
Do you feel like it's hard to initiate movements or actions, even when you want to do something?

Yeah... I mean, that's... that's exactly what I've been trying to say. It's exactly like I was saying before about sitting on my mattress in these same gray sweatpants and this blue camp shirt. It's... it's like I just can't make myself do anything anymore. The want to do it might be there, buried somewhere way, way down deep, but the bridge between wanting to do it and actually moving my body to do it is just... gone. It's completely gone. 

Like I was saying about the knitting and the journaling. I used to love those things. I still look over at that basket of mustard-yellow yarn sometimes, and maybe a tiny part of me remembers that I was making a scarf, and maybe I even think, "I should finish that scarf before winter." But then... nothing happens. My arms don't move. My hands don't reach out. I just sit there. It's not that I'm frozen or paralyzed, it's just that the energy required to lift my arm, to close my fingers around the wooden needles, to loop the yarn... it feels like trying to move a mountain. It feels impossible. 

And it's not just hobbies. It's everything. It's the walking I used to do down at the park under those big oak trees. I haven't been down there in weeks. I haven't even gone downstairs to get a glass of water sometimes, even when my throat is so dry it hurts to swallow, because standing up and walking down the fourteen carpeted stairs to the kitchen is just too much. I can't initiate it. I can't start the process of moving. 

And then my mom comes in, like I told you, and she stands there in the doorway, and she asks me what's wrong. And I know I should answer her. I know I should tell her I love her, or tell her I'm sorry, or just say *something* so she stops looking at me with that awful, worried crease between her eyebrows. I want to reassure her. I really do. But I barely have the energy to open my mouth. I barely have the energy to form the words. I just look at her, and my head feels heavy, and I can't make myself speak. I just can't make myself do anything at all. So, yes, it's incredibly hard to initiate any kind of action. It's the hardest thing in the world right now.
Do you feel like your body movements have become slower than they used to be?

I don't... I don't think they are. Not the movements themselves, no. I know I just talked a lot about how hard it is to actually start moving, but once I finally do, if I absolutely have to, my body works exactly the way it always has. It's not like I'm walking through molasses or taking these tiny, slow-motion steps like you see in movies or something. 

Like, just the other night, I think it was Tuesday night because I could hear Mr. Henderson next door dragging his heavy plastic trash cans out to the curb, which he always does on Tuesdays right after dinner. Anyway, I finally had to get up to use the bathroom across the hall. I had been sitting on my mattress in the exact same spot for hours, just staring at the wall, but my bladder was hurting and I couldn't ignore it anymore. When I finally forced myself to stand up, I didn't do it in slow motion. I just pushed myself up. And I walked across the bedroom, right past my desk with the dusty pens, and I opened the door. 

I walked down the hallway at the exact same pace I did back when I was in high school. The floorboards creaked in the exact same spots. There is this one board right outside the linen closet that always groans if you step on it, and I walked right over it at a completely normal speed. When I reached out to turn the bathroom doorknob, the brass one that has always been a little loose, my hand didn't take ten seconds to travel through the air. It just reached out, grabbed the metal, and turned it. 

So the actual physical speed of my body, the mechanics of my legs and my arms, they aren't slow at all. It is really just the getting started part that feels impossible. Once the engine is actually running, the car goes the normal speed limit, I guess. I just... I just never turn the key anymore. So someone might look at me and think I am moving slow because I am just sitting here so incredibly still for hours on end, but if you actually watched me walk to the bathroom or reach for a glass of water, you would see that the movement itself is completely normal. It really hasn't slowed down at all.
Do you think your life will ever get better?

I don't... I don't really see how it could. I mean, when I try to picture tomorrow, or next week, or next year, or even ten years from now... it just looks exactly like today. I just see myself sitting on this exact same mattress. It has this floral fitted sheet on it that my mom bought at Target maybe three years ago, back when I was still in high school, and it has these little pink and yellow roses on it that are all starting to fade because it's been washed so many times. I just picture myself sitting on those faded roses, wearing these exact same gray sweatpants, staring at the exact same patch of beige carpet near the closet door. You know, where the vacuum cleaner left those parallel lines the last time my mom came in to clean, which was probably two weeks ago now. The lines are still there because I never walk over that part of the floor. 

People always talk about the future like it's this... this destination, you know? Like you pack a bag and go somewhere new and exciting. But for me, time just kind of washes over me while I stay completely still. I don't have a job to go to. I finished high school, and that was just... it. The conveyor belt just stopped moving. And now I'm just in this room. 

So how could it get better? If I can't even initiate the movement to pick up my knitting needles, like I was telling you, or go downstairs for a glass of water when I'm thirsty... how am I supposed to build a whole life? My mom sometimes leaves these pamphlets on my nightstand, right next to that really bright red digital alarm clock I mentioned earlier. She leaves brochures for community college classes, or volunteer programs at the animal shelter down on 4th Street, because she thinks if I just see them, I'll suddenly snap out of this and want to do things. She even folds the corners down on the pages she thinks I'll like, making these little dog-ears. But I just look at the glossy paper and I feel absolutely nothing. There's no spark. There's no pull towards any of it. It's just paper sitting on wood. 

So when you ask if it will ever get better... I just don't have any reason to believe that it will. I don't have any evidence that things change. It just feels like this is how it is now. This is it. Just me, the mattress, the closed blinds, and the sound of the cars out on the street that I'm never actually going to go out into. I don't think it's ever going to be anything else.
Do you feel like your body physically moves more slowly than it used to?

Wait, didn't... didn't you just ask me that? About moving slower? I thought I just... I mean, like I was saying just a minute ago about walking down the hall to the bathroom, no. No, my body doesn't physically move slower. 

I know I might look like I do, because I'm just sitting here so much of the time, but... well, it's like I told my mom when she asked me almost the exact same thing. She was standing by my bedroom window, the one where the pull-cord for the blinds is all knotted up because our old cat chewed on it a few years ago, and she asked if my muscles felt stiff or heavy, like I was moving through water or something. And I had to explain to her, just like I'm trying to tell you again now, that the actual speed of my limbs is completely fine. 

If I accidentally knock my phone off the mattress—it has this really badly cracked glass screen protector on it from when I dropped it on the concrete driveway back before graduation—if it slides off the edge of the bed, I can reach out and catch it just as fast as I ever could. My reflexes aren't slow. My muscles aren't moving in slow motion. It's just the... the starting part that's broken, like I said. But the actual physical moving part, once it finally happens, is totally regular speed. I don't know if I'm just not making sense when I describe it, but yeah... no, my body isn't physically slower at all.
Do you feel like your body physically feels heavy most of the time?

Heavy? No... no, I wouldn't use that word to describe it. It doesn't feel like I'm carrying around extra weight or wearing a lead vest or anything. 

You know when you go to the dentist—like my dentist, Dr. Aris over on Elm Street, the one with the really old waiting room chairs that squeak—and the hygienist puts that heavy lead apron over your chest right before they take the X-rays? target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about cognitive slowing or slowed thoughts, which is not covered by my symptom profile (which only includes Negative Symptoms, Delusions, functional impairment, and duration).

patient.answer:
I don't... I don't think they're moving slowly. I mean, to have slow thoughts, you'd have to actually be having thoughts to begin with, right? And I just... I don't really have much going on up there to measure the speed of. 

When I'm sitting there on the edge of my mattress in these same gray sweatpants, just staring at the wall or looking over at that basket of mustard-yellow yarn, it's not like my brain is trying to process things and just taking a really long time to do it. It's not like when I was in high school and I'd be sitting in Mr. Harrison's algebra class, staring at a complicated equation on the whiteboard, and feeling like my brain was trudging through thick mud trying to figure out the answer. It's not like that at all. It's just... it's more like a blankness. 

Like I said before about my head feeling like it's full of wet sand, it's heavy, but it's not... it's not slow. I hear things right away. When my mom stands in the doorway with that crease between her eyebrows and says, "Honey, what's wrong?" I understand her immediately. The words don't take a long time to reach me. I process exactly what she's asking the second she says it. It's just that once the words land, there's no answering thought that comes after. There's just nothing. 

So I wouldn't say my thoughts are slow. I don't really notice them being slow at all. It's just that there aren't many of them anymore. I just sit there and look at the dust gathering on my desk, or the pens sitting in that mug, and my mind is just kind of... quiet. Not moving slowly, just... not really moving much at all, because there's nothing there to move.

doctor.question: Do you feel like it takes you a long time to react to things that are happening around you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about delayed reaction time or psychomotor retardation, which is not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I don't... I don't really think so. I mean, it's not like my reflexes are broken or I'm moving in slow motion or anything like that. I haven't noticed any kind of delay. 

Like, just yesterday afternoon, I was sitting on my mattress—right in the exact same spot I always sit, kind of near the window where the blinds are pulled shut because the glare from the street is always too bright—and my cell phone started ringing. It was sitting on the wooden nightstand right next to me, right beside this old digital alarm clock I've had since middle school, the one with the red numbers that are honestly way too bright at night. Anyway, the ringtone went off. It was just that loud, default chime, and I reacted right away. I turned my head the very second it started. I didn't sit there for a minute trying to figure out what the sound was. I looked at the screen immediately, saw it lighting up, and saw it was my Aunt Linda calling. She always calls on Tuesdays around three because she gets off work early from the dental clinic. 

I knew it was her, and I saw it instantly. I didn't answer it, obviously. I just watched the screen light up and vibrate against the wood until it finally went to voicemail. But the actual reaction? Noticing that it was happening? That was instant. If a car honks out on the street, I flinch just as fast as anyone else. If my mom drops a spoon on the linoleum in the kitchen downstairs, I hear the clatter right away and I know exactly what the sound is. There's no lag, you know? Like a computer freezing up or something. It's nothing like that. I see and hear everything in real-time, exactly when it happens. I just... I just don't have any desire to do anything about the things happening around me. But the reacting part itself doesn't take a long time at all.

patient.answer:
Yeah... I mean, that's... that's exactly what I've been trying to say. It's exactly like I was saying before about sitting on my mattress in these same gray sweatpants and this blue camp shirt. It's... it's like I just can't make myself do anything anymore. The want to do it might be there, buried somewhere way, way down deep, but the bridge between wanting to do it and actually moving my body to do it is just... gone. It's completely gone. 

Like I was saying about the knitting and the journaling. I used to love those things. I still look over at that basket of mustard-yellow yarn sometimes, and maybe a tiny part of me remembers that I was making a scarf, and maybe I even think, "I should finish that scarf before winter." But then... nothing happens. My arms don't move. My hands don't reach out. I just sit there. It's not that I'm frozen or paralyzed, it's just that the energy required to lift my arm, to close my fingers around the wooden needles, to loop the yarn... it feels like trying to move a mountain. It feels impossible. 

And it's not just hobbies. It's everything. It's the walking I used to do down at the park under those big oak trees. I haven't been down there in weeks. I haven't even gone downstairs to get a glass of water sometimes, even when my throat is so dry it hurts to swallow, because standing up and walking down the fourteen carpeted stairs to the kitchen is just too much. I can't initiate it. I can't start the process of moving. 

And then my mom comes in, like I told you, and she stands there in the doorway, and she asks me what's wrong. And I know I should answer her. I know I should tell her I love her, or tell her I'm sorry, or just say *something* so she stops looking at me with that awful, worried crease between her eyebrows. I want to reassure her. I really do. But I barely have the energy to open my mouth. I barely have the energy to form the words. I just look at her, and my head feels heavy, and I can't make myself speak. I just can't make myself do anything at all. So, yes, it's incredibly hard to initiate any kind of action. It's the hardest thing in the world right now.

patient.answer:
I don't... I don't think they are. Not the movements themselves, no. I know I just talked a lot about how hard it is to actually start moving, but once I finally do, if I absolutely have to, my body works exactly the way it always has. It's not like I'm walking through molasses or taking these tiny, slow-motion steps like you see in movies or something. 

Like, just the other night, I think it was Tuesday night because I could hear Mr. Henderson next door dragging his heavy plastic trash cans out to the curb, which he always does on Tuesdays right after dinner. Anyway, I finally had to get up to use the bathroom across the hall. I had been sitting on my mattress in the exact same spot for hours, just staring at the wall, but my bladder was hurting and I couldn't ignore it anymore. When I finally forced myself to stand up, I didn't do it in slow motion. I just pushed myself up. And I walked across the bedroom, right past my desk with the dusty pens, and I opened the door. 

I walked down the hallway at the exact same pace I did back when I was in high school. The floorboards creaked in the exact same spots. There is this one board right outside the linen closet that always groans if you step on it, and I walked right over it at a completely normal speed. When I reached out to turn the bathroom doorknob, the brass one that has always been a little loose, my hand didn't take ten seconds to travel through the air. It just reached out, grabbed the metal, and turned it. 

So the actual physical speed of my body, the mechanics of my legs and my arms, they aren't slow at all. It is really just the getting started part that feels impossible. Once the engine is actually running, the car goes the normal speed limit, I guess. I just... I just never turn the key anymore. So someone might look at me and think I am moving slow because I am just sitting here so incredibly still for hours on end, but if you actually watched me walk to the bathroom or reach for a glass of water, you would see that the movement itself is completely normal. It really hasn't slowed down at all.

doctor.question: Do you think your life will ever get better?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of hopelessness or pessimism regarding the future, which is not covered by the patient's symptom profile (Negative Symptoms, Delusions, Functional Impairment, Duration).

patient.answer:
I don't... I don't really see how it could. I mean, when I try to picture tomorrow, or next week, or next year, or even ten years from now... it just looks exactly like today. I just see myself sitting on this exact same mattress. It has this floral fitted sheet on it that my mom bought at Target maybe three years ago, back when I was still in high school, and it has these little pink and yellow roses on it that are all starting to fade because it's been washed so many times. I just picture myself sitting on those faded roses, wearing these exact same gray sweatpants, staring at the exact same patch of beige carpet near the closet door. You know, where the vacuum cleaner left those parallel lines the last time my mom came in to clean, which was probably two weeks ago now. The lines are still there because I never walk over that part of the floor. 

People always talk about the future like it's this... this destination, you know? Like you pack a bag and go somewhere new and exciting. But for me, time just kind of washes over me while I stay completely still. I don't have a job to go to. I finished high school, and that was just... it. The conveyor belt just stopped moving. And now I'm just in this room. 

So how could it get better? If I can't even initiate the movement to pick up my knitting needles, like I was telling you, or go downstairs for a glass of water when I'm thirsty... how am I supposed to build a whole life? My mom sometimes leaves these pamphlets on my nightstand, right next to that really bright red digital alarm clock I mentioned earlier. She leaves brochures for community college classes, or volunteer programs at the animal shelter down on 4th Street, because she thinks if I just see them, I'll suddenly snap out of this and want to do things. She even folds the corners down on the pages she thinks I'll like, making these little dog-ears. But I just look at the glossy paper and I feel absolutely nothing. There's no spark. There's no pull towards any of it. It's just paper sitting on wood. 

So when you ask if it will ever get better... I just don't have any reason to believe that it will. I don't have any evidence that things change. It just feels like this is how it is now. This is it. Just me, the mattress, the closed blinds, and the sound of the cars out on the street that I'm never actually going to go out into. I don't think it's ever going to be anything else.
